 Japan’s major tax change leaves Aussie travellers worse off
 Kristine Tarbert Updated November 8, 2026 - 11.33pm . First published at 11.19pm 
 shares Share article A major tax change has now come into effect in Japan, and it will impact Aussie travellers, especially if they love shopping .
 Japan remains one of the most popular overseas holiday destinations for Australians. In fact, the Japan National Tourism Organization recently confirmed the country was on track to welcome over 1 million Aussie visitors for the second year running.
 A major tax change in Japan will impact travellers who love shopping.  Getty Images/iStockphoto 
 Advertisement So what has changed? As of November 1, the tax-free status on shopping for overseas visitors has been updated. 
 You still won’t have to pay the tax, but it will be a more cumbersome process costing travellers more time and a little bit of extra patience.
 Previously, the 10 per cent GST was waived directly at the register if you showed your passport. But now you will have to keep all your receipts and submit them to customs for a refund.
 That means there will be a bit more admin involved on your part. It also means you’ll need to allow yourself more time at the airport when leaving.
 Read more
 Japanese city cracks down on bad tourist habit 
 Tax refund machines have been installed in airports, which is where visitors must head to before they check in their luggage. 
 After scanning your passport a green light means you’re clear. If you get a red light, customs needs to inspect your purchases. 
 That also means you won’t receive your refund immediately. Customs will first need to unlock the refund, and it will then be processed by the store back to the card used for the purchase.
 Advertisement Tax-free shopping in Japan isn’t going to be as easy as it has been,  iStock 
 That can take anywhere from three to 14 business days leaving visitors out of pocket.
 There is another option where travellers can use the Visit Japan Web site for tax-free shopping and claim their refunds before departure.
 It comes after the city of Tokyo announced it would increase its hotel tax , in direct response to overwhelming tourist numbers, adding hundreds of dollars to the cost of a holiday already.
 Advertisement Advertisement Starting from April 2027, the city will introduce a 3 per cent accommodation tax on hotels , meaning that for every night you stay, you’ll have to pay an increased fee per person per night.
 Currently, hotel guests pay a flat rate of ¥200 ($2) per person per night.
 Kyoto raised its accommodation tax in March 2026.  nna\chantelle.bozicevic 
 The city of Kyoto began charging an increased accommodation tax in March 2026. Travellers staying in luxury hotels (above $1000 a night) pay the most – ¥10,000 ($100) per night.
 Advertisement Rooms costing between $500 and $1000 per night incur roughly $40 tax each night, while those paying between $200 and $500 pay around $10 per night.
